definition: Repose means to rest or lie down.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word repose. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know repose should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: After the harvest feast, the whole household reposed on mats in the shade, and even the dogs stopped patrolling.
To lounge is to idle in a loose, slouchy sprawl; repose goes further into stillness — complete, composed rest.
Slumber goes past repose: the duchess reposing on the divan is awake and still, while a slumbering guest has crossed into sleep.

Rest is the plain, everyday word for stopping activity to recover — after practice, between shifts, on a park bench. Repose adds dignity and complete stillness to the same idea, which is why poems and portrait captions reach for it. A coffee break is rest; repose is rest held with composure.

To recline is specifically to lean the body back — an airline seat, a dentist's chair, an elbow sunk in cushions. It names a posture and nothing more. Repose names a state: complete, composed stillness, holdable in any position, carrying a quiet dignity that recline never claims.

Repose is rest in evening dress: choose it for portraits, poetry, and prose that wants dignity, and let rest or lie down do the daily work.

The retrospective's most famous photograph shows the ferry captain on the deck of her boat at dawn, hands folded on the rail.
The critics' word for it was repose: she is not asleep, not slumped, not even leaning — just completely, willingly still.
The photographer waited three mornings for that stillness.
On the first two, the captain kept checking the horizon and drumming her fingers.
On the third morning the fog delayed the crossing, and something in her settled.
The picture was taken in the four quiet minutes before the engines started.
Students who copy the pose always get the hands right and the stillness wrong; composure, the photographer liked to say, cannot be arranged.
